references.text: In the parable of the talents in [ref:Matt 25:27|Matthew 25:27], the Lord says almost word for word the same thing: "You should have put my money in the bank, so that when I came back, I could have received it with interest." This is the parallel text to Luke's parable of the minas.

[ref:2 Mos 22:25|Exodus 22:25] refers to lending with interest. The Mosaic law forbade Israelites from charging interest to one another, but the Lord's point in the parable is that the servant could at least have done the most basic thing with the money.

[ref:5 Mos 23:19-20|Deuteronomy 23:19-20] contains the law regarding interest (Hebrew: neshekh/tarbit). The law allowed charging interest from foreigners, but not from brothers. The Lord in the parable uses this well-known concept to show that the servant did not even do the least thing with what was entrusted to him.

[ref:Ordsp 14:23|Proverbs 14:23] says that "All hard work brings a profit, but mere talk leads only to poverty." The principle that effort yields return supports the Lord's expectation that the servant should have managed the money actively.

The context in [ref:Luk 19:20-22|Luke 19:20-22] shows that the lazy servant hid the mina in a cloth out of fear, and the Lord judges him by his own words. Verse 23 is the logical consequence: Even though the servant feared the Lord, he should at least have put the money in the bank.

[ref:Luk 16:10-12|Luke 16:10-12] deals with faithfulness in small things. Jesus teaches that whoever is faithful in little is also faithful in much. The Lord's criticism in Luke 19:23 targets exactly the lack of faithfulness even in the smallest stewardship task – putting money in the bank.
